aims: Apply conservation of energy to a planet that receives energy from its star and radiates energy into space.

slides.title: A planet is an energy budget
bullets: A planet gains energy from its star and loses energy to space, both as radiation
Absorbing more power than it emits: its internal energy rises and it warms
A warmer planet emits more, because emission grows as $T^{4}$
The temperature stops changing once the two powers are equal: radiative equilibrium
Every calculation in this topic starts by writing the two powers and setting them equal
slides.notes: Link back to B.1: a cup of tea on a table cools until it gives out energy as fast as it receives it. A planet does the same thing, with space as its surroundings and a star as its supply.

slides.title: The energy balance
bullets: True only when the temperature is constant
If the two sides differ, the difference is the rate of change of internal energy
slides.notes: Not in the data booklet: it is conservation of energy applied to a system. Ask what could upset the balance (a change in the star, in the reflection of sunlight, in the atmosphere). That list is the plan for the rest of the topic.

aims: State the meaning of the solar constant $S$ and calculate the intensity of a star's radiation at a given distance.
Explain why the intensity on the ground is lower at high latitudes.

slides.title: The solar constant
bullets: $S$: the intensity of the Sun's radiation at the Earth's distance, above the atmosphere, on a surface facing the rays
It is the Sun's apparent brightness as seen from the Earth (B.1)
Unit: $\text{W m}^{-2}$, so it tells us the power arriving on each square metre
Other planets have their own value: intensity falls with the inverse square of the distance from the star
slides.notes: Ask why the definition insists on "above the atmosphere" and "facing the rays". Each phrase removes something that would reduce the reading.

slides.title: Radiation from a star
bullets: Use the data booklet's value of $S$ for the Earth
$L$ is the star's power; $4\pi d^{2}$ is the sphere the power has spread over at distance $d$
slides.notes: $S$ is in the booklet's table of constants. The apparent brightness equation is the one from B.1.

slides.title: Why latitude matters
bullets: Two beams of equal power and equal width
At high latitude the same beam covers a longer stretch of ground, so each square metre gets less
It also crosses more atmosphere on the way
slides.notes: Shine a torch straight down on a desk, then tilt it. The lit patch gets longer and dimmer, with the same torch.

slides.title: Sunlight at Saturn
slides.question: Saturn orbits at a distance of $1.43 \times 10^{12}$ m from the Sun, whose power output is $3.8 \times 10^{26}$ W. Calculate the intensity of the Sun's radiation at Saturn, and compare it with the Earth's solar constant.
slides.hint: The power has spread over a sphere whose radius is the distance from the Sun. Use the apparent brightness equation.
slides.notes: Saturn receives about 1% of the intensity at the Earth. Saturn is about 9.5 times further away, and 9.5 squared is about 90: a quick way to check the answer.

points.guide: Emissivity as the ratio of the power radiated per unit area by a surface compared to that of an ideal black surface at the same temperature.
aims: Define emissivity and state its range of values.
Calculate the power radiated by a real surface, using $P = e\sigma AT^{4}$.

slides.title: Emissivity
bullets: A black body is the perfect emitter and absorber: nothing at the same temperature radiates more
Emissivity $e$ compares a real surface with a black body at the same temperature
No units, and between 0 and 1: $e = 1$ for a black body, close to 0 for a polished metal
A surface with $e < 1$ is sometimes called a grey body
Good emitters are good absorbers (at the same wavelengths)
slides.notes: A lamp-black sphere and the small hole in a hollow metal cavity are both close to ideal black bodies. A polished silver teapot keeps tea warm because it emits so poorly.

slides.title: Emissivity and radiated power
latex: e = \dfrac{\text{power radiated per unit area}}{\sigma T^{4}}
bullets: The first form is in the data booklet; $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-4}$
$T$ must be in kelvin

slides.title: From the definition to the power radiated
slides.start: Start from the definition of emissivity for a surface of area $A$ at temperature $T$.

steps.text: Emissivity compares the power per unit area with that of a black body
Multiply by the area to get the power radiated
Check: a black body has $e = 1$, which gives the Stefan–Boltzmann law

slides.notes: Students who remember the derivation need only one equation from the booklet.

slides.title: A wood-burning stove
slides.question: The outer surface of a cast-iron stove has an area of 1.5 $\text{m}^2$, a temperature of 230 °C and an emissivity of 0.85. Calculate the power radiated by the stove.
slides.hint: A real surface emits less than a black body, so include the emissivity. Convert the temperature before using it.
slides.notes: This is the power emitted, not the net loss: the room radiates back to the stove too. Using 230 instead of 503 would give a power about 23 times too small.

slides.title: Testing a black coating
slides.question: A laboratory test panel coated in black anodised aluminium has an area of 0.25 $\text{m}^2$. At a temperature of 400 K it radiates 320 W. Determine the emissivity of the coating.
slides.hint: Work out what a black body of the same area and temperature would radiate, then compare.

steps.text: Power from a black body of this size at 400 K.
Emissivity is the ratio of the powers.

slides.notes: No units. An answer above 1 would be a sign of a mistake, since nothing out-radiates a black body at the same temperature.

points.guide: Albedo as a measure of the average energy reflected off a macroscopic system.
aims: Define albedo and calculate the power a surface absorbs from its albedo.
Distinguish between albedo and emissivity.

slides.title: Albedo
bullets: Sunlight striking a surface is partly absorbed and partly reflected or scattered
Albedo $\alpha$: the fraction of the incident power that is scattered back
The fraction absorbed is therefore $1 - \alpha$
No units, between 0 and 1: a mirror is close to 1, and a black body is 0
Fresh snow scores high (about 0.85), desert about 0.4, forest about 0.1, ocean about 0.06
slides.notes: Walking barefoot on dark tarmac and on pale sand on the same sunny day shows the difference. The deck has a table and a satellite map of monthly albedo: good to show here.

slides.title: Albedo
bullets: In the data booklet
Power absorbed = (1 − albedo) × incident power

slides.title: Emissivity or albedo?
bullets: Albedo describes what happens to radiation arriving (visible and near-infrared from the Sun)
Emissivity describes the radiation a surface gives out because of its temperature (for a planet, infrared)
Snow reflects most sunlight (high albedo), yet it is an excellent emitter of infrared (high emissivity)
So $e$ is not simply $1 - \alpha$: the two numbers refer to different wavelengths
slides.notes: Fresh snow has an infrared emissivity of about 0.98 but a visible albedo of about 0.85. This example usually ends the confusion between the two ideas.

slides.title: Dust on a glacier
slides.question: Sunlight of mean intensity 650 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ falls on 12 $\text{km}^2$ of glacier during a summer day. A layer of windblown dust lowers the albedo of the glacier's snowy surface from 0.75 to 0.45. Calculate (a) the incident power and (b) the increase in the power absorbed.
slides.hint: Convert the area to square metres. The absorbed fraction is the part that isn't scattered, so find how much that fraction changes.

steps.text: (b) Find the change in the fraction absorbed.

slides.notes: That is about the output of two large power stations, spent on melting ice. Soot and dust on ice are a real and measured effect.

points.guide: Earth's albedo varies daily and is dependent on cloud formations and latitude.
aims: Explain why the Earth's albedo changes with cloud cover, latitude and season.

slides.title: The Earth's albedo changes
bullets: The Earth's yearly mean albedo is about 0.30
Cloud changes from day to day and is highly reflective
Latitude: polar snow and ice reflect strongly, and water reflects more when the Sun is low
Season and land use also matter: snow cover, crops, forest clearance
Finding one value for a whole planet is complicated, which is why satellites map it
slides.notes: Show the satellite albedo map from the deck and ask students to identify deserts, ice and cloud bands.

slides.title: Cloud over the ocean
slides.question: A model region is ocean of albedo 0.06, and any part covered by cloud has albedo 0.70. Sunlight of mean intensity 340 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ arrives from above. Calculate the albedo of the region on a day when cloud covers (a) 40% of it and (b) 50% of it, and (c) the change in the intensity absorbed between the two days.
slides.hint: Each part of the region contributes in proportion to its share of the area. Multiply each albedo by its fraction and add.

steps.text: (a) Combine the two albedos using area fractions.

slides.notes: Clouds also affect the infrared leaving the Earth, so their overall effect on temperature is more complicated than this.

points.guide: The incoming radiative power is dependent on the projected surface of a planet along the direction of the path of the rays, resulting in a mean value of the incoming intensity being S/4.
aims: Derive the mean incoming intensity $S/4$ from the projected area of a planet.

slides.title: Disc in, sphere out
bullets: A planet catches sunlight over its projected area: the disc $\pi R^{2}$ that makes its shadow
As it spins, that energy is shared over the whole sphere, of area $4\pi R^{2}$
The sphere has four times the area of the disc
So the mean intensity over the whole surface is a quarter of $S$
For the Earth, the mean is about 340 $\text{W m}^{-2}$
slides.notes: Hold a ball in the beam of a projector and look at its shadow on the wall. The shadow is a disc, not a sphere.

slides.title: Mean incoming intensity
bullets: Averaged over day and night, equator and poles
slides.notes: $S/4$ is a mean. Nowhere on the Earth actually has this as a steady value.

slides.title: Where the factor of 4 comes from
slides.start: A planet of radius $R$ is at a distance where the star's intensity is $S$.

steps.text: Power intercepted by the projected disc
Total surface area that shares this power
The $\pi R^{2}$ cancels, whatever the planet's size

slides.title: The projected area
bullets: Sunlight is blocked by the disc $\pi R^{2}$
It is spread over the sphere $4\pi R^{2}$

slides.title: Sunlight on the Moon
slides.question: The Moon has a radius of $1.74 \times 10^{6}$ m, and the solar intensity at its distance from the Sun is 1360 $\text{W m}^{-2}$. Calculate (a) the power of the sunlight intercepted by the Moon and (b) the mean intensity over its whole surface.
slides.hint: The Moon intercepts sunlight over its shadow disc. For (b), share that same power over the whole sphere.

steps.text: (b) Total surface area of the sphere.

slides.notes: The answer to (b) is exactly $S/4$, as the derivation predicts. The radius cancels, so it would be the same for any planet at this distance.

points.guide: Problems will include the estimation of equilibrium temperature of a body using energy balance between incoming and outgoing radiation intensity, including albedo, emissivity, and solar or other constants.
aims: Derive and use the energy-balance equation $(1 - \alpha)\tfrac{S}{4} = e\sigma T^{4}$.
Estimate the equilibrium temperature of a planet or other body, including albedo and emissivity.

slides.title: Energy balance for a planet
bullets: Set $e = 1$ if the surface emits as a black body
For a planet around another star or at another distance, use its own value of $S$
slides.notes: This combines several booklet relationships. It is not printed in the booklet in this form, so students should be able to build it.

slides.title: Finding the equilibrium temperature
slides.start: Apply the energy balance to each square metre of the surface, on average.

steps.text: In equilibrium, this equals the power emitted per square metre

slides.title: What the model gives for the Earth
bullets: With $\alpha = 0.30$ and $e = 1$, the model gives about 255 K (−18 °C)
The measured mean surface temperature is about 288 K (15 °C)
The 33 K difference is the natural greenhouse effect
A simple fix: give the Earth an effective emissivity of about 0.6
slides.notes: Let students calculate 255 K from the equation before showing it, then ask what the model has left out. That sets up the second half of the topic. The effective emissivity comes from the 238 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ absorbed divided by the 390 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ that a black body emits at 288 K, which gives 0.61.

slides.title: Tips for energy-balance problems
bullets: Start from $S/4$ for a rotating sphere; use $S$ alone only for a flat surface facing the rays
Multiply by $1 - \alpha$, not $\alpha$
Take the fourth root at the end: pressing the square-root key twice does it
Temperatures in kelvin; give °C only if asked
If a question gives total powers, the same method works with areas $\pi R^{2}$ and $4\pi R^{2}$

slides.title: Ceres, a dwarf planet
slides.question: The dwarf planet Ceres has no atmosphere, an albedo of about 0.03 and spins once every 9 hours. It orbits the Sun at 2.77 times the Earth's distance. Assuming it emits as a black body, estimate its mean surface temperature. Use $S = 1360\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ for the Earth.
slides.hint: First scale the solar constant using the inverse-square law. Then balance the absorbed and emitted intensities.

steps.text: Intensity at Ceres, using the inverse-square law.

slides.notes: Ask why the question mentions the fast rotation: it makes sharing the energy over the whole surface a reasonable assumption. With no atmosphere there is no greenhouse effect to add.

slides.title: A probe in deep space
slides.question: A spherical space probe of radius 0.60 m is at the Earth's distance from the Sun but far from the Earth. Its surface has an albedo of 0.40 and an emissivity of 0.80. The probe spins, so its temperature is uniform. Determine its equilibrium temperature.
slides.hint: Write the total power absorbed (over a disc) and the total power emitted (over a sphere) and set them equal. See what happens to the radius.

steps.text: Power absorbed, through the projected disc.
Power emitted, from the whole sphere.

slides.notes: The radius wasn't needed: a larger probe catches more sunlight and has more area to emit from. Spacecraft designers choose surface coatings to control $\alpha$ and $e$ separately.

slides.title: A snowball Earth
slides.question: Geological evidence suggests that the Earth was once almost entirely covered in ice, giving an albedo of about 0.60. Assume the mean incoming intensity was 340 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ and that the Earth had an effective emissivity of 0.61. Estimate the mean surface temperature in °C.
slides.hint: Find the absorbed intensity and set it equal to the emitted intensity. Remember the emissivity, and convert at the end.
slides.notes: A very cold, very reflective planet tends to stay that way: this is the ice–albedo feedback working in reverse. Volcanic CO₂ building up over millions of years is thought to have ended these episodes.

points.guide: Methane CH4, water vapour H2O, carbon dioxide CO2, and nitrous oxide N2O, are the main greenhouse gases and each of these has origins that are both natural and created by human activity.
aims: Describe the greenhouse effect in terms of the different wavelengths emitted by the Sun and the Earth.
Name the four main greenhouse gases, with a natural and a human source of each.

slides.title: The greenhouse effect
bullets: The hot Sun emits mostly visible and near-infrared radiation, and most of it passes through the atmosphere
The ground absorbs this radiation and warms, then emits infrared, because it is far cooler than the Sun
Greenhouse gases absorb much of that infrared, then re-emit it in all directions
Part of it returns to the surface, which settles at a higher temperature
The natural effect keeps the Earth about 33 K warmer, so liquid water and life are possible
slides.notes: Real greenhouses work mostly by stopping warm air from rising, so the name is misleading. Ask students what they'd expect at night on a clear sky compared with a cloudy one.

slides.title: The main greenhouse gases
bullets: Water vapour H₂O: evaporation; humans add little directly, but a warmer atmosphere holds more
Carbon dioxide CO₂: respiration, volcanoes, decay; fossil fuels, deforestation, cement
Methane CH₄: wetlands, termites; cattle, rice paddies, landfill, gas leaks
Nitrous oxide N₂O: soil and ocean bacteria; nitrogen fertilisers, industry
Water vapour contributes most to the natural effect
Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of dry air, hardly absorb infrared
slides.notes: Each gas has both natural and human sources: students need one of each.

slides.title: The greenhouse effect, step by step
bullets: Step through the four numbered stages
The re-emitted infrared goes in all directions, not just down

slides.title: Radiation from a desert
slides.question: The ground in a desert reaches a temperature of 320 K at midday. Use Wien's law, $\lambda_{\text{max}}T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}$ m K, to find the peak wavelength it emits. Name the region of the spectrum, and state why this radiation behaves differently in the atmosphere from sunlight.
slides.hint: Rearrange Wien's law for the wavelength. Compare your answer with the wavelengths of visible light, and think about which radiation greenhouse gases absorb.

steps.text: This is about 20 times the wavelength of visible light: the infrared.
Greenhouse gases absorb strongly in the infrared but let most visible sunlight pass.

slides.notes: Even the hottest ground on the Earth emits far into the infrared.

points.guide: The absorption of infrared radiation by the main greenhouse gases in terms of the molecular energy levels and the subsequent emission of radiation in all directions.
aims: Explain the absorption of infrared by greenhouse gases using molecular energy levels.
Calculate the energy of an absorbed photon using $E = hf$.

slides.title: The energy-level picture
bullets: Molecules can only hold certain discrete amounts of vibrational and rotational energy
A photon is absorbed only if its energy $hf$ matches a gap between two of these levels
In greenhouse gases the gaps match infrared photons; visible photons do not fit
A photon of infrared is later given out as the molecule de-excites, in a random direction
Or it passes the energy to neighbouring molecules in collisions, which warms the air
slides.notes: Infrared photons are far too weak to move electrons between levels: this is about the vibration and rotation of the whole molecule. Electron transitions need visible or ultraviolet photons.

slides.title: Different gases, different wavelengths
bullets: Each gas absorbs only in particular bands of the infrared
Water vapour has the widest bands; carbon dioxide has a strong one near 15 µm
The Earth's emission peaks near 10 µm and spreads widely either side, so these bands intercept much of it
Some infrared escapes through gaps between the bands, the "atmospheric window"
slides.notes: The absorption charts in the deck are good to show here: ask which gas contributes most, and which contribute least.

slides.title: Photon energy
bullets: For radiation, the speed $v$ is $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

slides.title: A carbon dioxide absorption band
slides.question: Carbon dioxide absorbs strongly at a wavelength of 15 µm. Calculate (a) the frequency of this radiation, (b) the energy of one photon of it and (c) how many times more energy a photon of visible light of wavelength 500 nm carries.
slides.hint: Convert the wavelengths to metres. Find the frequency from the wave equation, then use the photon equation.

steps.text: (c) Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

slides.notes: A visible photon carries 30 times the energy of this gap, so it does not match and passes through.

points.guide: The greenhouse effect can be explained in terms of both a resonance model and molecular energy levels.
aims: Explain the absorption of infrared using a resonance model of a molecule.
Compare the resonance model with the energy-level model, including the limits of the resonance model.

slides.title: The resonance model
bullets: Treat a molecule as atoms joined by springs, so it has natural frequencies of vibration
For greenhouse gases these lie in the infrared, about $10^{13}$–$10^{14}$ Hz
Infrared radiation has an oscillating electric field that pushes on the molecule's charges
When the driving frequency matches a natural frequency: resonance, and energy is absorbed strongly
A molecule stores energy in vibration (kinetic and spring potential), and in rotation
Collisions then share it as translational kinetic energy, which is what a thermometer registers
slides.notes: A child on a swing, pushed at the right moment, is the familiar resonance example. Only vibrations that shift the charge distribution absorb: that is why N₂ and O₂, with no such vibration, hardly absorb infrared.

slides.title: How carbon dioxide vibrates
bullets: Bending and asymmetric stretching vibrations absorb infrared
In the symmetric stretch the charge stays balanced, so it does not

slides.title: Two models of one process
bullets: Natural frequency in the resonance model ↔ energy gap $\Delta E = hf$ in the energy-level model
The spring model is easy to picture, and links to oscillations in Theme C
It predicts that absorption would be spread around each natural frequency
It cannot explain why only certain sharp frequencies are absorbed
The energy-level model explains the sharp frequencies, using quantum ideas
slides.notes: The guide has a linking question on the limits of the resonance model: good for a short pair discussion. Is either model "the true one"?

points.guide: Energy balance problems will include energy exchanged between the surface and the atmosphere of a body.
aims: Use a Sankey diagram to show the energy flows between the surface, the atmosphere and space.
Solve energy-balance problems for the surface and atmosphere, and predict the effect of a change in the flows.

slides.title: Two systems exchanging energy
bullets: A better model separates the surface and the atmosphere; each obeys energy in = energy out
All flows are means, in $\text{W m}^{-2}$, over the whole planet
Sunlight is partly reflected, partly absorbed by the atmosphere, and the rest reaches the surface
The surface loses energy by infrared emission and by convection and evaporation
The atmosphere radiates both down to the surface and up to space
Check three places: the surface, the atmosphere and the top of the atmosphere
slides.notes: Deck slides 35–38 build the Sankey diagrams one arrow at a time, first with a non-greenhouse atmosphere and then with greenhouse gases. Drawing the pair side by side shows exactly what the greenhouse gases add.

slides.title: Balancing the surface
bullets: "Solar" is the sunlight absorbed; "losses" are convection and evaporation
The surface is usually treated as a black body at temperature $T_{\text{s}}$
A grey atmosphere at temperature $T_{\text{a}}$ emits $e\sigma T_{\text{a}}^{4}$ in each direction

slides.title: The surface with a grey atmosphere
slides.start: Model the surface as a black body. All the sunlight that isn't reflected reaches the surface, and the atmosphere is a grey body of emissivity $e$.

steps.text: Sunlight absorbed per square metre of surface
Power emitted by the black-body surface

slides.notes: In this simple model the surface loses energy only by radiation. Questions will state what to include.

slides.title: Tips for flow problems
bullets: Treat each system in turn: add up what goes in and what goes out
If the surface emission is shown as two arrows, add them before using $\sigma T^{4}$
Arrows from the surface that pass through the atmosphere count at the top of the atmosphere, not for the atmosphere
If in and out differ, the system gains or loses that much power per square metre, so it warms or cools
To find a new temperature, set the new emitted intensity equal to the new absorbed intensity

slides.title: Energy flows in the Earth system
bullets: Widths are to scale
Find the largest input to the surface: it is not the Sun
slides.notes: Back-radiation from the atmosphere is about twice the sunlight absorbed by the surface. That surprises most students.

slides.title: The Earth without greenhouse gases
slides.alt: Sankey diagram with arrow widths to scale, in watts per square metre. A band of 340 arrives from the Sun. 70 is reflected to space by clouds and 30 by the ground. The remaining 240 is absorbed by the ground. The ground emits 240 as infrared, which passes straight through the atmosphere to space.
bullets: Arriving: 340 $\text{W m}^{-2}$. Reflected: 70 by clouds and 30 by the ground
The ground absorbs 240 and emits 240 as infrared
With no greenhouse gases, all of that infrared escapes to space
A black-body surface emitting 240 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ would be at about 255 K, far colder than today's 288 K
slides.notes: Arrow widths are to scale. Check the balance at the top of the atmosphere: 340 in, and 70 + 30 + 240 = 340 out. Compare with the Sankey diagram of the real Earth on the previous slide. Check: $T = \left(\dfrac{240}{5.67 \times 10^{-8}}\right)^{1/4} = 255$ K.

slides.title: A planet without greenhouse gases
slides.question: On a model planet, the atmosphere contains no greenhouse gases. The mean incoming intensity is 410 $\text{W m}^{-2}$. Clouds reflect 90 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ back to space, the ground reflects 40 $\text{W m}^{-2}$, and the rest is absorbed by the ground. Determine (a) the intensity absorbed by the ground and (b) its equilibrium temperature, assuming it emits as a black body.
slides.hint: Sunlight is either reflected or absorbed. With no greenhouse gases, what the ground emits goes straight to space, so it must equal what it absorbs.

steps.text: (b) In equilibrium, the ground emits what it absorbs.

slides.notes: Check at the top of the atmosphere: in 410, out 90 + 40 + 280 = 410.

slides.title: Finding the missing flow
slides.question: In a model of the Earth, the mean intensities in $\text{W m}^{-2}$ are: 340 arriving from the Sun, 102 reflected, 78 absorbed by the atmosphere, and the rest absorbed by the surface. The surface emits 398 of infrared, of which 36 escapes directly to space, and loses 98 by convection and evaporation. The atmosphere radiates 336 to the surface. Find (a) the sunlight absorbed by the surface, (b) whether the surface is in equilibrium, (c) the intensity the atmosphere must radiate to space for it to be in equilibrium and (d) the surface temperature, assuming it emits as a black body.
slides.hint: Add up the energy going into and out of each system in turn. The surface's infrared that doesn't escape directly is absorbed by the atmosphere.

steps.text: (b) Surface: in equals out, so it is in equilibrium.
Atmosphere in, which must equal its total emission.
(d) All of the surface emission counts.

slides.notes: Finish by checking the top of the atmosphere: 102 + 36 + 202 = 340, equal to what arrives.

slides.title: More greenhouse gas
slides.question: In the model of the previous example, extra greenhouse gas raises the back-radiation from 336 to 342 $\text{W m}^{-2}$, while the other flows at the surface stay the same. Calculate (a) the net rate of energy gain per square metre of surface and (b) the eventual rise in surface temperature if the surface's infrared emission increases to restore equilibrium.
slides.hint: The surface was in equilibrium before, so the imbalance is only the change. Find the new emission and the temperature that goes with it.

steps.text: (b) The new surface emission must be 6 higher.
Original temperature, to the same precision.

slides.notes: Keep more figures here: rounding the temperatures to 3 s.f. too early loses the small difference. A 6 W m⁻² imbalance is only about 1.5% of the surface emission.

slides.title: A grey atmosphere on an exoplanet
slides.question: A model of an exoplanet has a mean incoming intensity of 510 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ and an albedo of 0.40. The atmosphere has an emissivity of 0.65 and a temperature of 260 K. All the sunlight that isn't reflected reaches the black-body surface. Calculate (a) the intensity radiated downwards by the atmosphere, (b) the surface temperature and (c) the rise in surface temperature if the atmosphere warms by 5.0 K.
slides.hint: The surface absorbs both sunlight and the atmosphere's downward radiation, and emits as a black body.

steps.text: Black-body surface: 302 K to 3 s.f., with more figures kept for part (c).
(c) Atmosphere at 265 K emits 181.8, so the surface absorbs:

slides.notes: Extra figures are kept because the rise is small compared with the temperatures. The extra 13 W m⁻² is only about 3% of what the surface absorbs, and because emission goes as the fourth power, a 3% rise in emission needs a rise of under 1% in temperature.

points.guide: The augmentation of the greenhouse effect due to human activities is known as the enhanced greenhouse effect. The burning of fossil fuels is a primary cause.
aims: Define the enhanced greenhouse effect and identify burning fossil fuels as its main cause.
Describe evidence for it, its feedbacks, its consequences and ways to reduce it.

slides.title: The enhanced greenhouse effect
bullets: The strengthening of the natural effect by human activities that add greenhouse gases
Burning fossil fuels is the main cause: it returns carbon stored for millions of years to the air as CO₂
CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm before industry to over 420 ppm, an increase of about 50%
The rise in CO₂ follows the rise in fossil fuel emissions
Global mean surface temperature is more than 1 °C above that of the late 1800s
slides.notes: The Keeling curve on the topic page is worth showing here. Ask students to explain the small yearly zigzag. Clarify that the ozone hole is a separate problem.

slides.title: Feedbacks and consequences
bullets: Positive feedbacks amplify warming
Warmer air holds more water vapour
Melting ice lowers the albedo
Thawing permafrost releases methane
Consequences include:
Warmer air and oceans; more frequent extreme weather
Rising seas, from melting land ice and thermal expansion
Changed local climates; more acidic oceans
slides.notes: Note that melting sea ice does not itself raise the sea level; melting land ice does. Thermal expansion of the water does too.

slides.title: Reducing the enhanced effect
bullets: Generate electricity from renewable and nuclear sources instead of fossil fuels
Use energy more efficiently, waste less and consume less
Use public and electric transport
Protect and replant forests; capture CO₂ from power stations
Large-scale change needs action by governments and international cooperation
slides.notes: Physics can predict outcomes, but it cannot settle who should pay. A short discussion here connects with the ToK questions on the page.

points.guide: Extra (from the teacher's deck): a simple spreadsheet model of how a system approaches equilibrium.
aims: Use a simple iterative model to show how a system approaches a new equilibrium, and why the response takes time.

slides.title: Modelling with a spreadsheet
bullets: Real climate models need supercomputers, but the central idea fits in a spreadsheet
A steady input plays the part of the power from the Sun
A loss that grows with the amount stored plays the part of radiation to space
Equilibrium is reached once the loss equals the input
Adding greenhouse gas is like reducing the fractional loss: the level climbs to a new equilibrium
slides.notes: A tank of water with a tap and a leak gives students something concrete to reason about before any spreadsheet appears.

slides.title: Building the model
bullets: Column A: the time step, with each cell one more than the cell above
Column B: the amount stored, starting at zero
In B3 enter =0.92*B2+6, for an input of 6 and a loss of 8% each step
Fill the formulas down for about 100 rows, then plot a graph of B against A
Change the input or the loss and watch the new equilibrium appear
slides.notes: Students can build this themselves in ten minutes. Ask them to predict the equilibrium first, then check it from the graph.

slides.title: A pond fed by a stream
slides.question: A new pond starts empty. Each day a stream adds 6 $\text{m}^3$ of water, and 8% of the water stored is lost by seepage and evaporation, so that $M_{\text{new}} = 0.92M_{\text{old}} + 6$. Determine (a) the volume of water after 3 days, (b) the equilibrium volume and (c) how long the pond takes to reach 95% of its equilibrium volume.
slides.hint: For (a), apply the rule three times. At equilibrium, the volume no longer changes, so what is lost equals what flows in.

steps.text: (a) Apply the rule, starting from zero.
(b) At equilibrium, 8% of the water equals the daily input.
(c) The gap to equilibrium shrinks by a factor of 0.92 each day.
Use logarithms, or read it from the spreadsheet.

slides.notes: The pond approaches equilibrium quickly at first, then ever more slowly. In the same way, the climate takes decades to respond fully to a change in the atmosphere.
